rationale: Start with a broad gradient at intermediate temperature to maximize the chance of observing all 10 compounds and reveal the retention range and critical separations. This scouting run will guide targeted changes in gradient slope, solvent range, and temperature.

Halve the gradient time to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin remains. Keep temperature and solvent endpoints fixed to isolate the effect of gradient slope.
The fast gradient eliminates the time penalty but leaves a tightly clustered group. Raise temperature to test whether altered selectivity can resolve that group without lengthening the run.

Use a slightly shallower gradient to improve the crowded separations, with temperature just below 60 °C to move away from its near-coeluting pair. The last peak should still elute near the zero-time-penalty region.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to seek a larger resolution margin while keeping the last peak near 8 minutes. This tests a neighboring method that may retain the maximum CRF with more robust separation.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a higher starting organic fraction as a nearby alternative that may shorten retention while preserving full resolution. Keep temperature and gradient duration fixed to assess this change.

Reduce the endpoint to make the gradient slightly shallower, aiming to restore the deficient separation from injection 6 while retaining its shorter retention times. This neighboring method may achieve CRF 1.000 with a more balanced resolution margin.

A further small decrease in gradient slope should lift the 1.47 critical resolution above 1.5 while keeping the last peak close to 8 minutes. This tests whether a more balanced separation can match the maximum CRF already achieved.

Test a 5 °C decrease from injection 4 to characterize temperature sensitivity around a maximum-scoring method. This isolates selectivity changes and checks whether full resolution persists at a lower temperature.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with the fast gradient to see whether the crowded group separates on the opposite side of its temperature-dependent crossover. This may provide another maximum-scoring method with a shorter elution time.

Preserve injection 4’s gradient slope of 0.075 organic fraction per minute and temperature while shortening the programmed gradient. All peaks previously eluted before this new gradient ends, so the maximum CRF should be retained.

Test a gradient slope between injections 7 and 8 to balance their two critical separations while bringing the last peak below 8 minutes. This may retain CRF 1.000 with slightly more resolution margin than injection 4.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to seek improved critical-pair resolution while keeping the last peak near 8 minutes. This explores another potential maximum-scoring method beyond the established 0.05–0.10 starting-fraction region.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a faster, hotter gradient for an alternative short-run separation. The combined changes may move the high-temperature near-coelution through an elution-order crossover and restore resolution.

Raise the starting organic fraction to test whether the remaining close pair in injection 14 separates further after its apparent elution-order crossover. Keep temperature and gradient duration fixed while seeking full resolution in a substantially shorter run.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to balance the two neighboring critical separations seen in injection 15. This tests whether the short-run, high-temperature branch can also reach full resolution and CRF 1.000.

Return to the maximum-scoring region with a slope between injections 8 and 12, aiming to balance their critical separations around R = 1.58. The last peak should remain below 8 minutes, preserving the zero time penalty.

Use a shallower gradient than injection 13 to improve its R = 1.19 critical pair while retaining the stronger separation of the other close pair. This may yield a larger minimum-resolution margin with no time penalty.

Slightly flatten injection 18’s gradient to raise its remaining critical resolution above 1.5. The last peak is projected near 9 minutes, testing whether this higher-starting-organic method can achieve full resolution without a time penalty.

Preserve injection 4’s initial gradient slope but switch to an earlier hold after the first nine peaks have eluted. This tests whether a lower final organic fraction can retain full resolution and keep the last peak within the zero-time-penalty window.

Preserve injection 8’s gradient slope and temperature while lowering the endpoint to 0.60. Since all peaks should elute before the gradient reaches its outlet endpoint at 8.65 minutes, this should retain its maximum CRF and minimum resolution of about 1.58.

Retain injection 4’s gradient slope and temperature while ending the gradient at 0.65 after 8 minutes. All peaks should elute before the outlet gradient ends, preserving CRF 1.000 with a lower endpoint and shorter programmed gradient.

Slightly flatten injection 21’s gradient to improve the earlier critical pair while testing whether the later pair remains above R = 1.5. The last peak is expected near 9 minutes, potentially retaining maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Test a gradient slope between the maximum-scoring injections 17 and 23. Their separation patterns suggest this method should retain all adjacent resolutions above 1.5 and keep the last peak below 9 minutes, preserving CRF 1.000.

Use a gradient slope between injections 17 and 24, both of which achieved CRF 1.000, with a lower endpoint and shorter programmed gradient. This final method should preserve full resolution and zero time penalty; the campaign has already reached the maximum possible score.
